observations.statement: The design is a three-arm field experiment randomizing at the couple level which spouse receives a maternal risk module on top of a family planning curriculum given to everyone; arms are laid out in a notation table.

The estimands are named explicitly: direct and spillover treatment-on-the-treated effects of informing each spouse versus family planning only, and the gender difference between them; the paper states that the control also attends a meeting so that meeting or demand effects do not confound the incremental effect of the risk module.
observations.quote: unambiguously isolate the incremental effect of maternal mortality information

observations.statement: Selection into attendance is addressed by a double-blind invitation (surveyors and invitation cards do not reveal meeting type) and by requiring both spouses to attend together, so TOT effects for men and women are estimated on directly comparable samples; the TOT estimand is written out in a footnote.

Randomization is stratified on seven baseline characteristics listed in the text; the paper notes that all drop-out between baseline and re-screening occurred before assignment and is therefore orthogonal to treatment.

A cheap-talk model yields four numbered implications (belief updating, heterogeneity by preference gap, fertility, transfers) and each empirical subsection is introduced as a test of a named implication.

Couples recruited from the catchment areas of two named public clinics in Lusaka via a random address generator; baseline survey dates, intervention rollout window and endline window are all stated; the unit is the couple (household outcomes) or the individual spouse.

Eight eligibility exclusion criteria are enumerated in a footnote, split between medically motivated ones agreed with ethics committees and ones tied to study objectives; participants of an earlier related experiment were also excluded.

The paper documents the loss of eligibility between baseline and re-screening, the addition of replacement couples with only a reduced wife-only baseline, the share of invited couples who attended, and the endline attrition rate.
Every regression table reports the number of observations per column; individual-level tables have roughly twice the rows of household-level tables because both spouses are stacked.
Because replacement couples lack a full baseline, a dummy for availability of baseline data is included as a stratification variable and wife reports are used for stratification when needed.

Outcomes are summarized as Kling, Liebman and Katz style indices averaging component variables standardized against the control group mean and SD within gender; sub-indices for risk factors and ladder-scale beliefs are defined with their survey items.
observations.quote: Index construction follows Kling et al. (2007) throughout the analysis

observations.statement: Treatment enters as two assignment indicators (husband treated, wife treated) and, for individual-level outcomes, interactions with a respondent-gender dummy so that direct and spillover effects are separate coefficients.

The primary fertility outcome is current pregnancy at endline combined with a ladder-scale likelihood of more children; birth spacing is set aside because gestational age is hard to measure within a one-year window.

Transfers are measured by an index built from husband-reported gifts (any and value) and wife-reported emotional support and satisfaction items, with the source respondent of each component stated in the table notes.
Household income used as a control is trimmed at the top percentile.
Contraceptive use data are described as inherently noisy because relevant variation is on the intensive margin, motivating their placement in an appendix table.

Main tables report the coefficients with SEs in parentheses and p-values in brackets, rows flagging stratification variables, demographic controls and respondent interactions, an F-test p-value for equality of the husband and wife effects, the control-group mean for non-index outcomes, and N; columns are different outcomes rather than a controls progression.
Each results table leads with the aggregate index in column 1 and then reports its components in subsequent columns.

Estimating equations are stated as OLS with a fixed control vector (spousal ages, education, number of children, age of last child, baseline contraception, income, stratification variables); no weights are mentioned.
observations.note: weights_stated used to record that none are mentioned

observations.statement: Standard errors are clustered at the meeting (workshop session) level as stated in table notes, but the text offers no explicit argument for this choice; randomization is at the couple level and sessions are the delivery unit.
Comparisons across arms and between direct and spillover effects are made via F-tests of coefficient equality whose p-values are reported in every table rather than by pooling arms.
Multiple outcomes are handled by aggregating into summary indices rather than by adjusting p-values; no multiple testing correction is mentioned.
Balance across treatment arms among attending couples is reported in an appendix table with individual tests and joint F-tests, and summarized in the text.
Differential attrition across arms at endline is tested and reported in an appendix table.
Belief updating is framed as the first stage of the information treatment and reported first, before behavioural outcomes.
observations.quote: the “first stage” outcome necessary for the information treatment

observations.statement: Reporting bias is addressed by re-estimating fertility outcomes using the untreated spouse's reports and noting the concordance of husband and wife answers, with the alternative estimates in an appendix table.
Post-double-selection LASSO over functions of stratification and demographic variables is run as a robustness check on control selection, reported in appendix tables.
observations.locator: Section 4.5, Appendix Tables A15 and A16

observations.statement: Heterogeneity results are re-estimated adding interactions of treatment with the baseline beliefs index (with missing-indicator imputation) to show that preference mismatch, not baseline beliefs, drives the pattern.
observations.locator: footnote 42, Appendix Tables A8 and A9

observations.statement: Index components are reported item by item in appendix tables so readers can see which curriculum elements drive the index results.
observations.locator: footnote 37, Appendix Tables A5 and A6

observations.statement: Heterogeneity in spillovers is estimated by interacting treatment indicators with three mutually exclusive baseline categories of spousal fertility preference gaps, presented as a figure of coefficients and tied to a model implication.
Heterogeneity by stratification variables for fertility and transfers is relegated to an appendix explicitly because those specifications are not tied to model predictions.
observations.quote: the specifications are not tied to clear predictions from our model

observations.statement: Learning by baseline correctness is examined by stacking risk-factor questions into respondent-answer observations and splitting by whether the baseline answer was correct, pooling genders to maximize power.
observations.locator: footnote 39, Appendix Figure A4, Appendix Table A7

observations.statement: An alternative explanation that men do not listen to women is probed using the fact that a female facilitator delivered the birth-spacing content, checking whether treated men learned that item.
The strategic communication mechanism is supported by showing heterogeneity in spillovers by the sign of the spousal preference gap, as the model predicts.
Self-reported communication with the partner about risk is used as an intermediate outcome linking belief spillovers to the transmission channel.
Wife-reported measures of husband preferences are validated by correlating them with a willingness-to-pay elicitation from treated women for their husband to be treated.
Effects on binary outcomes are interpreted as percentage-point changes relative to the control-group mean reported in the table.
Index outcomes are read in standard deviation units by construction; the text reports the index coefficient together with its p-value.
Insignificant estimates are discussed by point estimate sign and by whether equality with the other arm can be rejected, rather than treated as zero.
The authors state that because the control also receives family planning information, some effects may be harder to detect.
Endline beliefs measured one year out may miss short-run belief changes that drove behaviour.
Restricting to couples where both spouses attended may select more cooperative couples; the authors accept this for comparability across genders.
The conclusion notes that the design cannot separate the effect of learning in a gender-segregated peer group from the information itself.

Inclusion criteria are argued to select more cooperative couples, so the authors suggest patterns would be starker in the general population; the facilitator-gender argument is flagged as possibly domain specific.

Tables use no significance stars; SEs in parentheses and exact p-values in brackets under each coefficient; notes define every outcome, its source respondent, the control lists and the clustering; a baseline table compares women and men with difference SEs and p-values.
The single main-text figure is a coefficient plot of spillover coefficients across preference-gap subgroups; distributional shifts and descriptive figures are placed in the appendix.
observations.locator: Figure 1, Appendix Figures A1 to A5

observations.statement: Appendix tables and figures are numbered with an A prefix and a separate Appendix B holds additional heterogeneity discussion; theoretical proofs are in Theoretical Appendix A.
The introduction previews the full pattern of results across arms and then devotes separate paragraphs to contributions to four literatures and to policy.

Order is context with baseline descriptives, theoretical model, experiment (design, curriculum, recruitment, data, identification), then results ordered by model implication with a mechanism subsection inside the first results block; no separate robustness section.
Component-level results, heterogeneity, LASSO checks, balance, attrition and preregistered secondary outcomes are all in appendix tables referenced from the text and footnotes.
A formal model section with propositions and implications precedes the experimental design and is used to label the results subsections.
A data availability statement gives a Zenodo DOI for the data and code; supplementary data are said to be available at the journal site; intervention scripts are in supplemental materials.
No statistical software is named in the text.
All outcome data come from surveys the authors collected (baseline, immediate post-intervention elicitations, one-year endline), complemented by DHS statistics for context.

The trial is registered on the AEA RCT registry with the ID given; the text says the analysis follows the registration for the main families of outcomes and reports preregistered secondary outcomes in an appendix; three ethics approvals are listed with IDs and consent is mentioned for added couples.
Preregistered outcomes not featured in the main tables (contraceptive take-up, willingness to pay) are explicitly noted and pointed to an appendix table.

Implementation details to protect the design are described: different meeting types at different time slots, randomized slot assignment, facilitator rotation across arms, participants not told partner session content, attendance incentives.

gaps: No explicit justification for clustering at the meeting level
No multiple testing adjustment despite many outcomes (indices used instead)
Online appendix (Tables A1 to A16, Figures A1 to A5, Appendix B, Theoretical Appendix A) is not part of the text file; its contents are known only from in-text references

reading.note: All 31 pages of the extracted text read, including references. The online appendix is not included in the file, so appendix practices are recorded only as referenced from the main text.
